Plus: GoFundMe's playbook | Saturday, November 21, 2026
 
View in browser
 
PRESENTED BY INTEL
 
Axios AI+
By Ina Fried, Madison Mills and Maria Curi · Nov 21, 2026

👋 Happy Saturday! Brad Olson here, taking the reins for a special weekend edition of AI+.

  • I've been wanting to write about the fringes of the AI adoption curve. So today I'm digging into how AI is transforming experiences as varied as playing Roblox and organizing on GoFundMe.

This newsletter is 1,285 words, a 5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Video games' massive AI experiment
By Bradley Olson
 

Illustration: Allie Carl / Axios
 

A deep, reflexive backlash against AI-generated writing, music and advertising is sweeping through the creative world.

  • But on Roblox, one of the world's most popular online videogame hubs, machine-assisted creation appears to be winning, and the players don't seem to mind.

Why it matters: The contrast offers a glimpse into the future of entertainment. Although audiences still demand human authenticity in traditional art, video game players have shown a pragmatic willingness to accept AI — as long as the result is fun.

The big picture: Roblox is becoming a real-time laboratory for the AI era.

  • A staggering 80% of its top 100 games in October were built with AI tools.
  • And although some of its 138 million daily users fear the proliferation of homogenized game clones, the ease of building new worlds and games with friends is showing millions a new dimension in the AI creation wars.

Yes, but: There is a well-documented psychological penalty for any kind of content that uses AI.

  • A 2025 NYU study found that fully AI-created ads achieved up to 19% higher click-through rates than human-created ads. But a simple disclosure of AI's involvement caused clicks to plummet 31.5%.
  • The pattern is repeating everywhere. A viral Spotify hit "I Run" sparked a listener revolt when fans realized the vocals were synthetic. A number of acclaimed novels have been pulled from shelves when authors were suspected of using AI.
  • People clearly enjoy AI-assisted content. They just hate knowing it. Our psychology holds human creation of art as sacred.

State of play: Roblox is a glaring anomaly. The platform is experiencing an explosion of AI-assisted creation, and a massive user base appears to be leaning in rather than logging off.

  • More than 500,000 users have already tried "Build," Roblox's natural-language creation environment that was released in a limited number of markets. They published over 70,000 games in the process.
  • Since the second quarter, time spent using AI tools has tripled among its top creators.
  • In September, a game created almost entirely with AI broke into the platform's top 10 by concurrent players.

What they're saying: "My advice to folks is this is a technology that's here to stay, and it's evolving incredibly quickly," Vlad Loktev, Roblox's chief creator officer, tells me. "In the future, everyone's a builder."

  • The platform's success with AI stems from fundamentally lowering the barrier to creation, he says.
  • "When I look into the future … we're going to have multiple millions of people who couldn't make games before, and now suddenly they can," Loktev says. "Just imagine the summation of all the creativity that those people are going to have."
  • He waves off the idea that AI games are inherently low-effort. Loktev notes that he is personally "over a thousand prompts deep" into building his own game and is also building them with his children. "It still requires a lot of effort on the creator's side to design something that's actually fun. Because right now, models can't tell you what fun is."

My thought bubble: I've seen this dynamic play out with my own sons, who like many young people are AI power users yet are distrustful about AI creation.

  • Building games on Roblox has helped sell them on the future of AI, especially as they imagine how it may democratize all software.
  • My younger son, Clark, 16, is building a game he hopes to launch in the coming months, but Soren, 18, mostly wants to make games he can play with his friends. His crew of gamers enjoy building games together as much as playing them.
  • Even as they enjoy it, they are wary of how the platform is changing. "The problem now is that there are a lot of games that are going by monetization trends," says Soren, who has played Roblox since he was 7. "You'll see a lot of the same type of game becoming popular over and over again."

As in other arenas, AI is capable of bringing every good and bad thing to pass.

The bottom line: The broader gaming world is currently enjoying Grand Theft Auto VI, a title some players view as the last great, entirely human-made blockbuster.

  • But on Roblox, a major transition is already underway. The machines are helping people build, the players are playing, and a new generation of gamers is learning to enjoy creating as much as consuming.

2. How AI fixed the fear of asking for GoFundMe
By Bradley Olson
 

Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Betty Laura Zapata / Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Asking for money is a barrier many prospective GoFundMe users never overcome, but CEO Tim Cadogan says the giving platform is cracking the code on getting more people to take the leap.

  • The secret was breaking down a fundraising campaign into a sequence of steps. GoFundMe spent nearly a year launching an AI coach that is now driving record donations.

Why it matters: Deconstruction is a hidden key to AI adoption. As GoFundMe surpasses $50 billion in total funds raised, its approach to AI implementation is a blueprint. By focusing on specific pain points — like writing a headline or setting a financial goal — the company's AI tools have already been used more than 100 million times.

The big picture: In a conversation with Axios, Cadogan discussed GoFundMe's AI strategy, the psychology of asking for money and how he uses AI as a sounding board for sensitive executive conversations.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Axios: GoFundMe took 10 years to raise the first $10 billion and just six more years to raise the next $40 billion. How does AI fit into that?

  • "At its root, the whole organization is focused on helping people help each other. That basically starts with the act of asking for help. As humans, we do not like asking for help at all. Functionally it's fairly easy, but psychologically and emotionally, it is a mountain to climb."

Axios: How does AI help someone figure out how to ask for money?

  • "Over the last three years, we noticed exactly where people dropped off. One drop-off was when people finished writing their story and had to come up with a title. Summarizing something painful, like an illness or cancer diagnosis, into a headline is daunting."
  • "Through AI, we read the story, look across tens of millions of past fundraisers, and suggest three titles. Over 80% of people take or modify them, and [the fundraisers] perform better."
  • "A second stopper was the financial goal. People wonder whether to ask for $2,000, $5,000, or $10,000. We introduced smart goals, which recommends a target based on historical patterns."

Axios: What is the financial impact of using AI to coach people through creating a fundraising campaign?

  • "We originally estimated the smart fundraising coach would generate $125 million in incremental help this year, but it is actually on track to double that — more than a quarter of a billion dollars."

Axios: As a CEO, how do you personally use AI to manage your day-to-day?

  • "A significant portion of my job is communication. I will draft a rough talk track, feed it my historical materials, and ask AI to evaluate and score it out of 10 on logical rigor, flow, resonance, and emotional connection to our customers."
  • "Across GoFundMe, about 95% of our staff use AI weekly. Being disciplined and systematically documenting decisions makes it much easier for AI systems to give you leverage. Chaotic underlying processes yield chaotic AI outputs."
